analysis.one_liner: Rewards states that ban tobacco sales to minors and raises the cigarette tax to pay for it.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in August 1989 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it died without a vote or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have paid states up to $200 million a year to pass laws banning tobacco sales to minors, tobacco vending machines where children are present, free cigarette samples, and smoking by minors in schools and on school buses. It also would have raised the federal cigarette tax slightly — from $8 to $8.50 per thousand cigarettes — with the increase funding a new trust fund to pay those grants. It was introduced in the Senate in August 1989 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it never received a hearing or vote before Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, children and teenagers would have gained the most: harder-to-buy cigarettes, no free samples, no tobacco vending machines where children are allowed, and smoke-free school buildings and buses. Parents would gain from less secondhand smoke around their kids. States would have received up to $200 million a year in federal grants to pass and enforce these laws, and adult smokers would have faced a small tax increase of 50 cents per thousand cigarettes (about 6%).

how_it_helps.text: It offers states $100 million a year in incentive grants to pass laws banning tobacco sales to minors, banning vending-machine sales where minors are present, and banning free tobacco samples.

It offers another $100 million a year to states that prohibit smoking by minors in school buildings, on school grounds, and on school buses, and that require separate adult smoking areas to protect students from secondhand smoke.
It funds a federal outreach program to inform minors of the health consequences of smoking.
It raises the federal cigarette tax from $8 to $8.50 per thousand small cigarettes and directs the revenue into a dedicated trust fund that pays for the grants.

analysis.who_pays: Smokers would bear the small tax increase; tobacco manufacturers, retailers, and vending machine operators would face the tax and lost sales from restrictions on youth access and free samples.

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by a federal cigarette tax increase, a regressive levy that falls hardest on lower-income smokers, who disproportionately smoke.
The trust fund and grants are still subject to annual appropriations Acts, so the promised $200 million a year could be reduced or withheld by later Congresses.
Federal grants condition state action on federal rules and federal compliance determinations, which shifts policing of retail sales and school conduct into a federal-state enforcement bureaucracy.
The bill explicitly permits adult smoking areas on school property rather than banning adult smoking on school grounds outright, a compromise that still exposes students to some secondhand smoke.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — fewer underage smokers and less secondhand smoke around children — are broad and would come largely from a small cigarette tax increase and from states' own laws. The drawbacks are real but modest: the tax is regressive, falling hardest on lower-income smokers, and the grant design keeps federal money flowing to states through existing channels rather than paying for new services directly. On balance the bill was a modest, well-targeted public health measure whose cost to smokers and manufacturers was small relative to the $60 billion in health and productivity costs cited in its own findings.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred the bill to the Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 3, 1989 by Senator Lautenberg, joined by Senator Hatch, and read twice in the Senate.
That same day it was referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over tax and health financing matters.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and it received no floor vote in either chamber before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
The bill never advanced beyond introduction and referral and so never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and retailers were better off, since the modest tax increase and the youth-access restrictions never took effect; states and teenagers gained nothing either way.

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal restrictions on tobacco marketing, vending machines, and cigarette taxes during this period, the standard industry posture against youth-access and tobacco-tax legislation.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor, but no committee or floor votes were ever taken, so no party split can be measured.

industries.note: A higher federal cigarette tax and state laws restricting sales to minors, vending machines, and free samples would shrink sales to the underage customers the tobacco industry relied on. The bill's own findings note the industry spends over $2 billion a year promoting its products.
States would have to bar tobacco vending machines wherever minors are allowed in order to qualify for grants, cutting off a sales channel.
